answerBody:
The governing rule should be the size-neutral rewrite of the 1994 transmission pricing policy, not the 20-megawatt incremental-cost floor. The two rules answer different questions. Only the rewrite prices the cost that ordinary customers already absorb when a computational load uses the existing network and also causes new facilities.

FERC’s October 26, 1994 policy statement, published November 3, 1994, at 59 Federal Register 55031, treats charging both an embedded-cost rate and an incremental-cost rate for the same service over the same facilities as unjust and unreasonable. The lawful charge is the higher of the two. That rule was built to open the grid to competing generators without collecting monopoly rents. Ari Peskoe’s reading, reported by Utility Dive, is that the premise fails for data centers. Embedded costs are a contribution to the network everyone uses. Incremental costs are the facilities the load causes. They are not two measures of one scarce path. S. 5653 section 2107 would legislate that finding under Federal Power Act sections 205 and 206, require FERC within 270 days to charge computational loads both costs, credit incremental payments to the annual transmission revenue requirement so other customers are not billed twice, and offer a lower rate for non-firm service. There is no megawatt cutoff.

Grid Strategies’ November 2, 2026 paper estimates about $55 billion over ten years under that rewrite, roughly $35 billion embedded and $20 billion incremental, and about $35 billion more than current policy, for about 40.3 gigawatts outside ERCOT. Those figures are assumptions, not statutory findings, and they exclude off-grid projects. They still show where the household exposure is. The 20-megawatt floor bars shifting incremental generation, storage, transmission, and distribution costs of covered loads, and it requires financial assurances if the load exits early. That is a real stranded-cost protection, and states may charge more than incremental cost. It does not, by itself, make a large load pay its share of the embedded grid. A hyperscaler that takes the higher of the two transmission charges can still socialize the other. The floor is also partly state-implemented. Grid Strategies treats full nationwide implementation as an upper bound of about $136 billion, not a forecast.

The strongest counterargument is that “and” pricing double-counts capacity, which is exactly why FERC rejected it in 1994, and that a size-neutral rule reaches small computing sites while missing the generation and distribution subsidies the floor targets. The credit to the revenue requirement answers the double-recovery objection on the utility side. A cutoff would invite splitting projects below 20 megawatts. Generation and distribution assignment can remain a state floor. It should not displace the federal transmission rule.

Congress should enact the size-neutral transmission pricing rewrite as the governing cost rule before the new Congress convenes. The 20-megawatt floor is a useful supplement, not a substitute.
rationale: The size-neutral rewrite is the governing rule because it prices both embedded network use and incremental transmission, which the 20-megawatt floor does not. FERC’s 1994 higher-of policy, the section 2107 credit against the revenue requirement, Peskoe’s distinction between the two cost categories, and Grid Strategies’ November 2, 2026 estimates support that choice. The floor remains a useful stranded-cost supplement, not a substitute. The word-counting capability confirmed answerBody is within range.
